en: Preface to the Traces of the Way of Yongming:

The sentiments of sentient beings cling to objects everywhere; the Bodhisattva’s teaching transforms them by dismantling these attachments everywhere. It is like an infant afflicted with illness who is harmed by milk;

when a skilled physician examines and diagnoses the condition, he stops the milk and administers medicine, and the disease is immediately cured. Furthermore, if the illness has persisted for a long time...
It is distressing. When one is harmed by medicine, the wise person recognizes this and dispatches the physician to discontinue the medicine; thus the ailment is also cured accordingly.

Nevertheless, this does not negate that milk has the benefit of nourishment, nor that medicine has the efficacy of healing. To cease using milk is a provisional measure, yet if it were universally abolished, those who would starve to death would surely be numerous.
Dispatching the physician is temporary, yet if physicians were dismissed as a general rule, those with chronic and deep-seated illnesses would certainly have no hope of recovery.
How fortunate! The remedies of the Three Vehicles are the sublime medicine for treating afflictions.
The convergence of all virtues is the milk that nourishes the Dharma-body. To stagnate in them is to obstruct right knowledge and vision; therefore, Bodhidharma descended [to China].
All [concepts] are beyond words and thought; they are eliminated through cessation. Yet, to discard them would contradict the gate of perfect interfusion.

Therefore, Great Master Yongming succeeded [to the lineage], harmonizing both phenomena and principle, and took this as his personal model. This Great Master was the legitimate grandson of Fayan and the true son of Master Shao.

He attained a wondrous realization of the single transmission and personally received the prediction of enlightenment. Nevertheless, while the Chan school does not rely on written texts, the Master delighted in...

The Chan school speaks of unimpeded eloquence as vast as a hundred volumes of flowing rivers, yet the Master sat in *paryaṅka* for ninety days; the Chan school scorns sitting meditation, yet birds nested in his robe-sleeves.

The Chan school points to the resolution that "mind-only" is all, with no other pure land, yet the Master practiced walking meditation and recited mantras. The Chan school shows people the way like a tiger among its peers, yet the Master taught that all virtues converge in one path, remaining diligent in practice.

The Chan school values only the correctness of the eye, not the cultivation of conduct, yet the Master [demonstrated] that all good deeds return to the same source. Through diligent effort, he showed that the myriad practices are of one essence.

He practiced the one hundred and eight [recitations] to suppress emptiness and excess, demonstrating the necessity of defensive embankments to guide those relying on the causal stage toward the ultimate fruit.

Like pure gold refined from the smelting furnace to create magnificent ornaments, or like the great ocean swallowing all streams without declining even a single drop, he was a true patriarch who attained great perfection—a holy Dharma King and a venerable Golden Wheel-turning Monarch.
After the Great Master entered nirvana, he was enshrined in a stupa at Daesimsan.
The temple was named Shouning. Having fallen into ruin and been submerged by time, its site had reverted to laypeople.

A monk of Jingci Temple named Monk He, who had long cherished the traces of this legacy, sought it out with great longing amidst the overgrown weeds and brush. Eventually, he recovered the śarīra relics.

When the monastics and the laity came to gaze upon and worship them, it was as if the sun of wisdom had reappeared after a lingering, heavy mist. They collectively deliberated on building a stūpa behind the Dharma Hall to solemnly enshrine the offerings.

I have compiled these supplementary records of his legacy and appended illustrations and eulogies, titling the work *The Traces of the Way of Yongming*. May it be circulated among the fourfold assembly. Alas!
Amidst the vast waves and white surges, his sacred remains remain intact north of the lake and south of the Xiang River; the design of the stupa remains unchanged.
Regarding the seven-jeweled reliquary of King Aśoka and the single-pointed awl of the Ancient Buddha—before the incense is added, let us all fix our gaze upon them.
Written on the day of the full moon in the early summer of the Dingwei year of the Wanli era by the Layman Tao Wangling,
a resident of Xie-an, at the Tiantai Monastery (Tianyi Jingsha) on Mount Falu in Kuaiji,
following the traces of the Way of Yongming.
Catalogue of the Footprints of the Yongming Lineage, compiled by Dahe,
Dharma Grandson of Yunsun at Jingci Temple (collated with the Six-Dream Layman Yu Chunxi and the Layman Ayong Huang Ruheng).
In total there are thirty-two accounts: the Eternal Radiance True Image,
the Manifestation of the True Image, the Response of the True Image, the Pacification of Filial Piety, the Cessation of Strife, the Flock of Sheep Listening to the Sūtra,
the Presentation of a Rhapsody at the Golden Gate, Releasing Living Creatures Despite Legal Prohibition, and the Magnanimous Pardon.
Renouncing the secular world to become a disciple, he cast aside the nest of a quail and donned the robes of a monk;
relying upon the prophecies of the sages, he was granted the lotus flower and protected by divine beings.
Secretly receiving the nectar of the Dharma, Xuedou instructed the assembly, reviving Lingyin and founding Jingci.
Yongming ascended the seat; Huatai recited the scriptures; Biefeng practiced the Way;
Yingta built a stupa to subdue the tides; ancient Buddhas mutually verified one another;
Goryeo sought refuge; Tiantai preached the precepts; food was offered to ghosts; and others were exhorted to recite the name for rebirth.
He subdued malevolent spirits and manifested the Dharma through falling flowers; he foreknew the arrival of his time and left auspicious signs during his cremation.
Lord Yan paid homage to his image, and a pheasant chick listened to his teachings.
He propagated the Confucian arts while temporarily manifesting the traces of an immortal.
End of the *Catalogue of the Path of Yongming*.
Lu Shusheng offers this eulogy:
I bow my head to the Wisdom-Awakened One, hailed as the Great Hero; His numinous roots are preeminent and surpass those of the divine child.
The ocean-treasury of all Buddhas is truly infinite; Even the treasury of the Lotus Sūtra is difficult to exhaust.
Since you, Master, have already finished explaining its meaning, Recite it so that the flock of sheep may kneel and listen.
To serve as their guardian forever, there is no need for national stores; If one sacrifices life to redeem life, what fear can one have of execution?
Facing the marketplace with joy, as if ascending to the sublime; the ruler was moved to realization and released his shackles.
Not only did he escape punishment, but he escaped the world as well. Releasing life is already a high way to deliver living beings;
all the dharmas possessed by the Tathāgata are summarized within the person of the Master alone.
May Amitābha’s aspiration for the stūpa be boundless;
From each stūpa, immeasurable light is emitted, Assisting that Compassionate Honored One with his white jade-like countenance, Enabling those in this Sahā world to know how to face the west.
Upon a distant peak, the Master recites the Buddha’s name, And conch shells and celestial music arise in the air.
The Mirror of the School opens its case to illuminate distant lands; the Kings of Goryeo gaze from afar.
Golden-threaded *kāṣāya* robes and amethyst beads, A golden *kamaṇḍalu*—these offerings are presented by this extraordinary nation.
Both the underworld and the celestial realm pour forth their devotion; May all those who take refuge throughout the ten directions contemplate thus.
Feng Mengzhen’s eulogy says: "The spirit in relation to the physical form is like spring in the branches of a flower. When spring ends, the flowers wither; when the spirit departs, the form perishes.
A master craftsman, such as those of the Song dynasty who carved jade into petals, might even deceive the eye of truth, making it appear as if by transformation.
Is there any skill in such craftsmanship? Duke Ye once excelled at painting dragons, yet upon seeing a true dragon,"
They flee in terror. A painted image is inherently insufficient to embody true life, let alone the state of non-arising (*anutpāda*).

Master Shou’s [statues] are not like this. They are like the divine *maṇi* jewel: neither form nor emptiness, neither arising nor ceasing; they radiate brilliance throughout both the hidden and the manifest, raining down all manner of precious treasures.
When one contemplates the most profound depths, such as the decaying realms of the underworld, or the skulls of those killed by Yama, [the Master’s images appear].
I constantly unfurl this portrait to offer my sincere devotion. I know that you, Master, have profoundly realized non-arising;
by means of the arising of the non-arisen, you deliver infinite sentient beings, yet without the mark of delivering beings. Is this not indeed the wondrous characteristic of Master Yongming?
The Chan Master Zhijue of Huiri Yongming Monastery in Hangzhou during the Five Dynasties period was named Yanshou, styled Chongxuan, and known by the sobriquet Baoyizi.
He was originally a native of Danyang, later moved to Yuhang, and settled there. His father was Lord Wang, and his mother was of the [blank] clan.
When he was able to speak, his teacher had him sit upon a high couch. Upon seeing his parents’ eyes turn against each other in conflict, he leaped down from it and knelt weeping on the ground.
His parents were moved to joy, and they remained together forever like the harmony of lute and zither.
Cáo Xuéchuān’s eulogy says: When the Master was still a child, he already knew how to sacrifice his life to move and transform those to whom he was indebted.
Later, when he ascended to the rank of Dharma King and became a tamer of the multitudes of spirits, it was because his power of advancement had its own source.

As the Sūtra says: "The *piṅgala* bird, while still in its egg, surpasses all other birds in song; the *śarabha*, upon emerging from the womb, strikes terror into all beasts with its majesty. This is indeed the nature of things.
There are those endowed with celestial endowment; I, having been born, wish to accomplish for the future what belongs to today, yet the passing of time still lingers.
Beholding the youthful purity [of the Buddha], how could I not feel shame regarding my own lack of virtue?

When the Master was still in his youth, he turned his heart toward the Buddha Vehicle. He abstained from pungent roots and meat, eating only one meal a day, and upheld the Lotus Sūtra, reciting seven lines at once.
Every time he unrolled the scroll, he was moved by the sight of a flock of sheep kneeling to listen.
Ge Yinliang said: "Regarding this very matter, there are certain clever and sharp-witted people who, upon hearing these words, do not believe them;

yet look at this dull-witted creature, and it instead possesses a profound point of entry—how truly strange! Looking further down, we find the parrot attaining the fruit of enlightenment and the earthworm preaching the sutras.
The more minute the being, the more its spiritual powers are manifest. Yet even these still belong to the realm of sentience."
This is not yet extraordinary. As for the "stubborn rock nodding its head," it truly startles people.
From this, observe closely: is the one preaching the Dharma truly Master Shou? And is the one listening to the Dharma still a sheep? Heh!
The spring colors of the Imperial Garden have already dawned; flowers and birds are all pleasing to the eye.
At the age of sixteen, the Master was a Confucian scholar. At that time, Emperor Wénmù of Wúyuè, Yuánhuān, was stationed in Hángzhōu.
The Master presented him with the "Fu on the Equal Heaven" (Qítiānfù). The assembly recognized him as a talent of extraordinary caliber and all wished to appoint him to office.
Huang Ruheng’s eulogy says: "Is he one who relies on the Buddha? He has personally presented himself at the golden gates. Is he one who takes Confucianism as his school? Who would name him a śramaṇa?
His mind and spirit are such that he leaps eastward and ascends westward. A master of Wu and Yue, a sovereign of Qing and Tai.
May he enjoy the longevity of the Heaven among heavens; may his life be immeasurable and without name. If one seeks his name, it shall be Maitreya, entering to succeed [Śākyamuni]."
He was accorded a position of high honor; indeed, there was not so much as a speck of dust separating Confucianism from Buddhism.
The Master once served as a storehouse clerk in Yuhang and later was transferred to the post of Garrison Commander in Huating, where he oversaw the collection of military supplies.

On several occasions, he used treasury funds to purchase fish, shrimp, and other creatures to release them back into the wild. When the matter was discovered, he was sentenced to death and led to the marketplace for execution.
Yu Chunzhen said: "If things and self share the same substance, why does one release life only to encounter death?

If they are not of the same substance, how can one enter death and be born again? Thus, the laws of the state and the teachings of the Buddha become distinct. Yet, the person of ultimate realization has no self."
"Only compassion is truly embraced. For him, even a gnat was regarded as a Great Awakening; facing the Gaofang Street execution ground was like encountering a *nirmāṇa-ratna-pura* (an illusory city).
Song Xu praised him, saying:
"Facing execution with such resolute spirit, his mind was naturally liberated; it would have been no hindrance for him to spend much money on releasing living beings."
The King was moved by compassion and granted him further honor, whereby he was able to transmit the lamp of the Dharma and continue the ancestral assembly.
While the King of Wu-Yueh was traveling upon the river, he dreamed that an old man led forty thousand fish and shrimp to him, saying, "These were all released by the tax collectors;
I pray that Your Majesty will spare them from punishment. Upon waking, the King sent men to investigate, just as the Master was nearing death.

The Master’s countenance showed no sign of distress. The official in charge of the execution found this strange and questioned him. The Master said, "I have not used a single cent of the treasury for my own private purposes;
I am merely redeeming a life. Now that I am to die, I shall surely be reborn directly in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss in the highest grade.
Why, then, should I feel any sorrow? The searchers reported this back to the king, who released him.
Su Zizhan’s *Zhilin* says: "A Chan master should receive ordination in a public execution ground;

therefore, a Bodhisattva manifests in such a place to deliver him, teaching the method of exiting death and entering life so that he may undergo one journey through the realm of death, which is equivalent to three thousand years of cultivation.
Since I have been exiled to the sea, I am somewhat closer to the realm of death, and my mind is filled with considerable anxiety."
I vow to follow the example of Master Yongming Shou by practicing the release of living beings (*fangsheng*) to realize the fruit of Arhatship. With deep reverence,

I have used the hairpins and earrings left behind by my deceased mother, Lady Cheng of Shu Commandery, to purchase the release of all creatures, thereby dedicating the merit toward the posthumous blessings of my parents.

From childhood, the Master had resolved to leave the household life, but his parents would not permit it. He therefore abstained from meat and pungent roots, and even drew blood from his own heart to moisten his brush and transcribe scriptures, vowing to fulfill his aspiration until the end.
When he reached the age of thirty, the King of Wuyue, recognizing the Master’s devotion to the Way, granted his wish and allowed him to become a monk.
He abandoned his wife and children and went to Longce Monastery, where he received the tonsure and ordination under the Chan Master Cuiyan.
Observing the precepts, he labored to provide for the assembly, completely forgetting his own person. His clothing was not of silk or cotton; his food lacked rich flavors.
With wild vegetables and coarse cloth tunics, he passed the days and nights.
Pan Zhiheng praised him, saying: "I have observed those of worldly wisdom and eloquence who wish to sever their mundane ties yet remain unable to do so until their hair turns white;
and those who leave their parents to enter the monastic life yet remain immersed in worldly attachments, causing their dark karma to deepen day by day.
As for our Master, when he presented his compositions at the Golden Gate, he was already hailed as a talent of rare caliber; while serving in the military of Huating, he had long since..."

A preeminent talent who emerged like a blade from its sheath, yet at the very age when one should be in the prime of his career, he finally severed the hair of affliction to become a Dharma minister on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, spreading transformation in foreign lands.
Alas! What a true hero among men this Master was!
The Master once practiced meditation in seclusion at Zhizhe’s Rock on Mount Tiantai. He remained in the lotus position without rising for ninety days.
A bird resembling a lapwing nested within his robes to raise its young; only after he emerged from meditative absorption did it depart.

Jinxue Zeng said: "Master Shou’s incident regarding the sparrow’s nest in his robes at Tiantai was a state of inconceivable realization within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), similar to the Tathāgata’s experience of a magpie nesting upon his head.

This is not something easily attained by those who have not forgotten their sensory faculties and whose minds have not become as still as wood or stone. It is just like the pigeon that took refuge within the shadow of the Tathāgata."
There is no fear or alarm. Is this not Zhuangzi’s metaphor of the sandpiper? I have not yet reached that realm and cannot offer a single word of praise;
only by being unable to offer a single word of praise can one perceive the wondrous inconceivability of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
What do those with the discerning eye think of this?

The Master arose from meditative concentration and immediately went to Mount Tiantai, where he attended upon National Teacher Deshao with the etiquette of a disciple, serving him as his teacher to the north.
At that time, the National Teacher’s vision encompassed both gods and men; upon seeing the Master at first glance, he deeply esteemed him and secretly transmitted the Mind-Seal to him.
He then said to the Master: "You have a karmic affinity with Yuan-shuai; in the future, you shall greatly propagate the Buddhist teachings. It is a pity that I did not live to see it."
I have seen the ears.
Langshi (Langzhong) wrote the "Eulogy on the Whale" in the Wu dialect:
"The Dharma King expounds the Dharma, which also relies upon the power of the Dharma; it is like the wind beating upon the void, as if aided by wings."

Master Shao reveals this prophecy: the conditions for the Dharma were planted long ago. As the successor to the spiritual tradition of Vulture Peak who now presides over Nanping, you are the descendant of the Bamboo Patriarch and the Tuozi lineage;
the world partakes in your virtue. Unbroken through great kalpas, where conditions and conditions are empty and still, the fire is transmitted when the fuel is exhausted.
I pray that you, Moon of Wisdom, will grant me your instruction.
While circumambulating at Guoqing Temple in the middle of the night, the Master saw that the lotus flower held by Samantabhadra suddenly appeared in his own hand.
Reflecting on his two long-held vows, he was undecided as to which path to take. He then ascended to Zhiyi’s Chan Hall and prepared two slips for divination:
one read "Single-minded Meditative Concentration" and the other "Various Good Deeds for Rebirth in the Pure Land. With a focused mind, he prayed: "Between these two paths..."
That which is easily accomplished requires seven attempts. One should pick it up with the hand of faith, doing so for as many as seven times without any interval.
Thus, one should single-mindedly cultivate the practice of pure karma.
The Bhikṣu Hong’en praised this, saying: “When the mind desires to be born in heaven, one dreams of soaring lightly;
when the mind dwells upon the Buddha-lands, the sacred realms manifest in the darkness. To dream of excrement and filth is to obtain wealth; to dream of coffins and vessels is to obtain rank.

These are signs of the correctness or inversion of one’s worldly and world-transcending thoughts. That the Master Fang experienced such auspicious responses while practicing the Way—truly, how universal!”
The Venerable Master is the teacher of the myriad practices; the lotus flower symbolizes the Dharma of the One Vehicle.
Could this not be the mark of the Master’s merit reaching the stage of True Purity, serving as the first omen for the realization of the wondrous and perfect fruition?
Throughout his life, the Master constantly established halls for the Lotus Repentance wherever he stayed to adorn the Pure Land.

Day and night, during the six periods, he universally performed the Lotus Repentance on behalf of all sentient beings in the Dharma-realm. Later, while he was establishing an altar at Guoqing Temple to perform the rites, he saw a divine being enter holding a halberd.
The Master rebuked him, saying, "How dare you enter without permission? The being replied, "I have long accumulated purity..."
Karma. Only now does one arrive within this state.
Zheng Hui praised him, saying:
"The Master performs repentance for all sentient beings—who then performs repentance for the Master? The vast and long night has not dawned for a thousand ages."
The Dharma Master Yugong carved these models for us; Master Jiegong and Master Hekong assisted in their production.

Were the sages of the Nine Mounds to rise again, the dark pearl would shine with brilliance. Lofty is the Flower Terrace, vast is the Dharma Treasury—vaguely, yet clearly, I behold the hand-holding lotus, the budding tusks of the elephant.
The Master once traveled to Mount Tiantu at Jinhua, where he recited the Lotus Sūtra for three years.
One night, while in meditative concentration, he saw Avalokiteśvara arrive through the air and pour nectar into his mouth.
From that time on, he attained unimpeded eloquence, and his writings filled scroll after scroll.
Jiang Pao’s eulogy says: If you say there is a Dharma difficult to cultivate, try practicing austerities for three years.
If you say there is cultivation difficult to realize, try investigating a single drop of sweet coolness. When the quail builds its nest, the master’s true nature is revealed.
"Three years are but a single day. The chick stood and transformed, manifesting the master’s wisdom-body. "A single drop fills a thousand rivers. This is what is called the Wondrous Dharma.

In the second year of the Guangshun era of the Zhou dynasty, the Master preached the Dharma at Mount Xuedou in Mingzhou; students flocked to him like the spokes of a wheel. The Master ascended [the seat].
The Master said: "At this place, Xuedou, a torrential waterfall plunges a thousand fathoms without halting for even a moment;
wondrous cliffs rise ten thousand cubits with no place to set foot. Where, then, do you all take your next step? At that time, a monk asked: "Xuedou’s single path—"
"How does one practice? The Master said, "At every step, cold flowers form; in every word, there is ice to the very bottom.

Wang Shizhen, courtesy name Yuánměi, wrote in the Preface to his *Xīn Fù* (Treatise on the Mind): "The ancient masters of India preached the Dharma for forty-nine years, yet in the end, not a single dharma was preached.
When one has not yet awakened, ten thousand words are not too many; when one has awakened, even a single [word]..."
The characters are not few. Alas! Why is it that this aged man speaks so much? This is indeed for the sake of the ground of those who study.
Throughout forty-nine years of preaching the Dharma, there is but one teaching, yet the various sutras give it different names.
If students of the Way merely pursue these names, they will only drift further away from the truth.
In the first year of the Jiànlóng era, the great donor Qian Zhōngyì, Prince of Wúyuè, seeing that Línghǐ Temple was in a state of ruin, requested the Master to restore it.

He rebuilt the halls and buildings, totaling over one thousand three hundred rooms, along with surrounding corridors on all four sides, extending from the main gate all the way to the abbot’s quarters, with passages connecting left and right. Thus, the Chan Master truly became the restorer of Línghǐ.
The Patriarch of the Restoration.

Monk Zhuhong praised it, saying: "The kalaviṅka’s song from Vulture Peak and the merit-water of Cold Spring—Amitābha himself has flown here, where several clusters of blue lotuses embrace the emerald green.
Moved by this, King Aśoka ascended to the high station of Saṃyaksambuddha."
Ascending the tower, the sun hangs over the vast blue sea; preaching the Dharma, the rain falls upon the Wu Mountains. To this day, the direct pointing remains unslanted;
the single mirror and two lakes have no front or back.
In the first year of the Xiande era, the King of Wuyue, Zhongyi, established Yongming Chan Monastery (which is the present-day Jingci Monastery) by imperial decree.
He bestowed the title of Chan Master Zhijue upon him and commanded him to serve as its abbot, becoming the first patriarch. He synthesized the three Buddhist schools;

his collected works include the *Zongjing lu* (Record of the Mirror of the Source) in one hundred fascicles, the *Wanshan tonggui ji* (Collection on the Universal Return of Myriad Good Deeds), the "Fu on the Spirit Dwelling in An-yang," the "Fu on the Mind," and various poems and gāthās.
In ninety-seven fascicles, it was included in the Great Canon for circulation. During the fifteenth year of the Yongming era, he personally ordained more than two thousand disciples.
Those who succeeded to his Dharma were Master Jin of Qianming Temple in Hangzhou and Venerable Zimeng of Fuyang.
Yu Chunxi’s eulogy says: Outside the gate is a lake; atop the hall is a single mirror. Within the mirror, the beauty of Xi Zi shines;
upon the lake, the rhinoceros horn flower reflects. To mistake this for a layered penetration is to allow the Dharma-eye to be clouded by the disease of cataracts.
What is the purport of Yongming? Who occupies the realm of Zhijue? He drags back the long-eared, scabby child and startles the ashes.
The Master ascended the seat before five hundred venerable monks.
A monk asked, "What is the wondrous purport of Yongming? The Master said, "Add more incense. The monk said, "Thank you for the instruction, Master.
The Master said, "Be glad that there is no connection at all. The monk bowed; the Master said, "Listen to this verse: "Desiring..."
I have long understood the purport of Yongming’s teachings: "Before one's door lies a lake; when the sun shines, radiance arises; when the wind comes, waves stir.

As transmitted by the words of Great Master Zibo, for a long time now, Chan and the Teachings (Dharma) have been mutually antagonistic, and the schools of Nature (Xing) and Characteristics (Xiang) have harbored mutual suspicion.
Only Master Shou’s *Zongjing Lu* (Record of the Source-Mirror) encompasses the Tripitaka and harmonizes the Five Schools; thus, its volumes number in the hundreds.
Scholars for the most part gaze out at the vast ocean in bewilderment. When they observe this Master ascend the seat, he directly picks up the entire lake of Xi Zi and hurls it onto the dais.
The wind stirs and waves arise; the sunlight shines and life is born.

To speak of it as Chan or as Teaching, as essence or as appearance, as inference or non-inference, as Consciousness-Only or non-Consciousness-Only—once one engages in such deliberation, one has already entered the ghost cave of the black mountains. It is not so.
The essential meaning of the Yongming era is thus established; how much more so for the various schools’ doctrines, which are but mere traps and snares?

Only those who possess the single eye can truly perceive this Mirror of the School. When Boya broke his strings and Jangseok laid down his axe, I cannot help but feel deep sympathy for these two masters upon reading these words.

To the west of Huiri Peak (Wisdom Sun Peak), there is a cavernous grotto where mountain and lake reflect one another. Every day the Meditation Master would recite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* at this cliff;
in total, he disseminated the teachings by reciting it thirteen thousand times. He once moved the various devas to rain down flowers.
The platform retains its original name.
Li Peizan said: "To insist on Chan while disparaging the teachings is called folly; to be mired in the teachings while scorning Chan is called madness.
Although the faults of such madness and folly are minor, they differ from no other views in that their resulting cycles of rebirth are indistinguishable.
My teacher [taught] that Chan penetrates the mind-only nature, realizing the fundamental emptiness of even a single word. The sutras proclaim the Supreme Vehicle, reaching [this same realization]."
The unimpeded nature of the ocean-treasury—this is likely what the heavens signify by raining down flowers, manifesting the wondrous cause of the perfection of both understanding and practice.

While Master [Zhili] resided at Yongming, he daily recited one hundred and eight items of scripture without ever faltering for a moment; when evening came, he would always go alone to a separate hall.
He practiced the *fengxingdao* (peak-circumambulation) nianfo. Those who followed him in secret numbered several hundred at all times.

On clear nights when the moon was bright, the sounds of conch shells, celestial music, and drums were occasionally heard in the sky. When King Zhongyi heard of this, he sighed in admiration, saying, "From ancient times, there has never been one who sought the Western Paradise with such earnest devotion.
He then specially constructed the Xiangyan Hall for the Western Paradise at Chijia.
Yan [did this] to fulfill his aspirations. Tu Benjun praised him, saying:
"The Chan Master’s Way was lofty and his virtue was flourishing; he was a master of the Fayan school.

Yet he personally practiced the one hundred and eight matters day and night. Through his practice of the Way, celestial music was heard in the void; through his recitation of the Buddha’s name, he moved the king."

Praising his virtues: To enter directly into the ocean of Samantabhadra’s tireless practices is, as the Master once praised, to illuminate ten thousand ages and serve as a "Second Saṃghavarman" for rebirth; these words are not flowery exaggerations.

As for those today who disparage meritorious practice while discussing the fundamental essence, or who rely on provisional skillful means while aspiring for the ultimate reality—does their approach not differ significantly from the Master’s intent?
In ancient times, Qiantang was called the Rakshasa River. Its tides were as perilous as those of the Goudang Three Gorges.

During the reign of the Qian Wang of Wuyue, when he constructed the seawall to protect against the ocean, the labor proved difficult to complete; he once attempted to shoot the leading edge of the tide with ten thousand crossbows, yet could not ultimately suppress its force.
In the third year of the Kaibao era, the Master received an imperial decree to establish the Six Harmonies Temple at Mount Yuelun.
A pagoda was erected, nine stories high and over fifty *zhang* in height, to serve as a stabilizing talisman. From then on, the tides followed their ancient course.
The local residents were grateful for this, and Daozan came to honor them, saying: "In the past, Yang Hou ran rampant, recklessly invading the dwellings of the people along our shores."
The reincarnation of Shenlong was such that even ten thousand crossbows could not withstand him. As for the Master’s construction of the stupa, bows and arrows and the *stūpa* are but equal things;
yet, in essence, was it not due to the Master’s power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) that there was some unseen force supporting it?
Now the stupa is gradually decaying, while the tide daily surges across it. How can we obtain a donor to adorn this Many-Jeweled Stupa (*Prabhūtaratna*) as if it were newly opened?

The Eternal Radiance Path (concluding): Releasing life to redeem it from death;
ceasing slaughter to give rise to compassion; severing the calamity of burning and boiling; releasing the bonds of confinement in cages and nets;
